bibliography.note: Keast, A. (sole author); Environmental Biology of Fishes 5(4): 305–314, December 1980; title matches

claims.claim: in Lake Opinicon, cyclopoids, nauplii and Bosmina "fell rapidly in May – early June, and did not increase again until August" (abstract only)
claims.note: the abstract has these words (cyclopoids, their nauplii and Bosmina longirostris) and ties the fall to the rise and fall of young fish in the habitat

claims.claim: young yellow perch, pumpkinseed, bluegill and three other species began feeding at 4.5–6.0 mm on nauplii and cyclopoids of 0.1–0.3 mm and took cladocerans from 8–10 mm (abstract)
claims.note: the abstract agrees: six species of an open-water community (Perca flavescens, Percina caprodes, Pomoxis nigromaculatus, Ambloplites rupestris, Lepomis gibbosus, L. macrochirus) first fed on nauplii and small cyclopoids 0.1–0.3 mm long (less tail); 4.5–6.0 mm first-feeding larvae; fish 10–14 days after hatching and 8–10 mm took larger prey including several genera of Cladocera

claims.claim: the first food of every fish larva: nauplii, rotifers and small cyclopoids of 0.1–0.3 mm at 4.5–6 mm; cladocerans from ~8–10 mm
claims.note: the abstract names nauplii and small cyclopoids, not rotifers

claims.claim: Bosmina and Chydorus taken from ~8 mm
claims.note: the abstract says 'several genera of Cladocera' at 8–10 mm without naming them

claims.claim: pumpkinseed and bluegill < 75 mm take 76–91 % of their food from the vegetation, chydorids and small midges among it (Keast 1980 via the foodweb audit)
claims.note: probably misattributed: this paper covers the first weeks of feeding (larvae of 4.5–14 mm), and the paper's Table 3.6-2 credits 'below 75 mm SL mostly vegetation-dwelling non-snail prey (76–91 %)' to Mittelbach 1984
